claims.text: stope. is a fully vegan kitchen, but it is a small shared kitchen rather than a dedicated gluten-free facility. Gluten-free dishes are prepared alongside wheat-based items (ramen noodles, burger buns, baked desserts), so cross-contact is possible. No celiac-specific separation protocol is documented; if you have celiac disease, confirm preparation directly with the owners.

Savory dishes here lean on Japanese flavors (teriyaki Buddha bowl, Japanese curry, ramen) that typically use soy sauce. Most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat, so unless a dish is specifically made gluten-free, assume it may contain wheat-derived soy sauce. Ask whether a gluten-free tamari is used for any dish you order.
The cafe is 100% plant-based, so there is no animal-product cross-contact to worry about. The entire menu, including cheese, ramen broth, and desserts, is vegan.

Service is repeatedly described as friendly and accommodating; staff have custom-made off-menu drinks and confirmed details with customers before serving, which suggests they are open to dietary requests. Still, no formal allergen-handling procedure is documented, so celiac and severe-allergy diners should explain their needs clearly.
Gluten-free options are available and specifically praised by diners ('I love that they offer gluten-free food as well').
Fully vegan menu, so plant-based diners can order anything without checking for animal ingredients.
Welcoming, family-run service that customers describe as friendly and willing to make special accommodations.

Sushiro's own allergen guidance states that ingredients are handled in factories and stores alongside other allergens, so cross-contact is possible even when an item's recipe does not list wheat. As conveyor-belt sushi prepared in a shared kitchen with wheat-containing items, this location is not celiac-safe.

The plain sushi rice and most plain fish nigiri (such as salmon, tuna, and shrimp) without sauce are not made with wheat, but they are prepared in an environment shared with wheat-containing products.

The standard soy sauce provided at the table is brewed from soybeans and wheat, so it contains gluten. Celiac and gluten-free diners should bring their own tamari or gluten-free soy sauce, as the restaurant is unlikely to stock it.

Some plant-based items exist (for example inari and vegetable maki such as cucumber), but they are prepared and delivered in a fish- and seafood-heavy conveyor-belt environment, so cross-contact with animal products is likely. There are no documented vegan-dedicated preparation procedures.

No specific reports about how staff at this branch handle allergy requests were found. Sushiro publishes brand-wide allergen tables but relies on diners to check them and confirm details; for serious allergies, confirm directly with staff before ordering.

Sushiro publishes a detailed, regularly updated allergen chart covering the legally specified allergens plus additional recommended ones, marked per menu item, which lets diners check ingredients before ordering.
Ordering is done via a tablet/touch panel at the table, making it easier to review items and select specific dishes rather than relying only on what passes on the belt.

Specific gluten-free dishes are offered and clearly labeled (for example the gluten-free matcha pancakes), but the kitchen also fries and serves wheat-based items like burgers, cutlets and onion rings, and no source confirms a separate dedicated fryer or a celiac-safe protocol - so cross-contact in shared frying oil and prep areas should be assumed unless staff confirm otherwise.

At least one diner specifically came looking for a gluten-free restaurant and found options here, and reviewers note a gluten-free menu is available - but availability of GF items is not the same as celiac safety.

No source confirms whether the soy sauce or seasonings used here are wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so savory dishes (burgers, cutlets, curries, kara-age) should be treated as potentially containing wheat-derived gluten unless staff confirm a wheat-free soy sauce is used.
The entire menu is 100% plant-based - no meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey are used anywhere in the kitchen - so vegan cross-contact with animal products is not a concern here.

Allergy information is made available and dishes are clearly labeled - reviewers note, for example, that allium-free (onion/garlic-free) items are marked on the menu - though the restaurant states that allergen information does not guarantee against a reaction and asks customers to make the final decision themselves.
Fully vegan, 100% plant-based menu, so there is no risk of animal-product cross-contact for vegan diners.
Dedicated gluten-free items exist and are clearly marked on the menu, and the restaurant publishes allergen information.
Allium-free (onion- and garlic-free) options are clearly identified on the menu, which diners with those sensitivities appreciated.

This is a wagyu ramen and gyoza house, so wheat is central to the kitchen: standard ramen noodles and gyoza wrappers are made from wheat flour. Even though gluten-free noodles are offered on request, shared pots, water, and prep surfaces mean cross-contact is likely. Treat it as not safe for celiac unless staff can confirm a fully separate preparation.

The ramen and seasonings are soy-sauce based, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The menu mentions gluten-free seasoning options on request, but unless that is specifically confirmed for your dish, assume the default sauces contain wheat.

Plant-based dishes are advertised, but this is a beef- and broth-focused kitchen (wagyu steak, wagyu ramen). No information confirms separate utensils, grills, or pots for vegan items, so cross-contact with meat and animal-based broth is possible. Confirm preparation with staff.

Staff speak English and there is a full English menu, which makes it easier to discuss allergies directly. No specific allergy-handling protocol is documented, so explain your needs clearly and ask how each dish is prepared.
The restaurant states that gluten-free noodles and seasoning options are available upon request.
Specially crafted plant-based dishes are offered for vegetarian and vegan diners.
The broth is described as 100% chicken-based with no pork, and the wagyu is halal-certified, which can help diners avoiding pork.
English-speaking staff and a full English menu make it easier to communicate dietary restrictions.

No source documents a gluten-free protocol or how shared cookware is handled. As traditional shojin-ryori, dishes are generally light and plant-based, but gluten-containing items are common in this style of cooking — wheat-gluten products such as fu (wheat gluten / nama-fu) and seitan-like ingredients are staples of Buddhist temple cuisine, so individual dishes may contain wheat. Celiac diners should not assume the meal is gluten-free and must confirm dish by dish with staff.

Broths are made from kombu, shiitake, and soybeans, and soy-based seasonings are typical of shojin-ryori. Most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat, so seasoning here likely contains wheat unless a wheat-free tamari is specifically used. No source confirms a wheat-free soy sauce, so celiac diners should request an adaptation and confirm directly before dining.

Multiple sources confirm the cuisine uses no animal products whatsoever — dashi is drawn from kombu, shiitake, and soybeans rather than fish or meat — so the menu is fully plant-based and well suited to vegans.

As a Buddhist vegetarian (shojin-ryori) kitchen, the entire operation observes the rule that no animal products are used, lowering the risk of animal-derived cross-contact compared with a conventional restaurant.

No reviews or sources describe how staff handle specific allergy requests. The set menus change seasonally and reservations are required in advance, so diners with allergies (especially wheat/gluten) should call ahead to ask whether the meal can be adapted.
Entirely plant-based, animal-product-free shojin-ryori with plant-based dashi (kombu, shiitake, soybean) — a strong baseline for vegan diners.
Reservations are required in advance, which gives diners a natural opportunity to discuss dietary needs before the visit.

This is a ramen and gyukatsu (breaded, deep-fried beef cutlet) house, so the kitchen routinely handles wheat noodles, flour and breadcrumbs. There is a high baseline risk of gluten cross-contact in shared pots, fryers and prep areas, and no source documents a gluten-free protocol.

The core dishes are not gluten-free or celiac-safe: standard ramen noodles are wheat-based, gyukatsu is breaded and fried, and tempura is wheat-battered. A celiac diner cannot safely eat the signature menu here.

Ramen broths and Japanese seasonings of this style typically rely on soy sauce and/or miso, most of which contain wheat. No source confirms a wheat-free soy sauce or tamari is used, so assume the seasonings contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

Vegan ramen options are advertised at this location, but no source describes how the vegan dish is prepared. Because the kitchen is built around beef-bone broth, wagyu and shared cookware, vegan diners should ask whether the vegan ramen is cooked in separate water/pots and kept away from beef broth.
The Tabelog listing notes that allergy information is available, and the venue offers English menus and English-speaking staff, which makes it easier to discuss ingredients before ordering.

As a halal-certified kitchen, the group states that all ingredients, seasonings and cooking methods are vetted for compliance, indicating an ingredient-aware kitchen, though this is a religious-dietary standard and is not the same as gluten-free or allergen-free handling.
Entirely pork-free and halal-certified, with vegan and vegetarian options marketed at this branch, so the kitchen is used to accommodating dietary needs.
English menus and English-speaking staff make it practical to confirm ingredients and ask about cross-contact in person.
Halal certification means ingredients, seasonings and cooking methods are documented and vetted, so staff are likely able to answer specific ingredient questions.

The menu is built around wheat-heavy American comfort food: buttermilk pancakes, burgers, and similar dishes are the signatures here. A kitchen that turns out pancakes, burger buns, and battered items shares prep surfaces and equipment, so cross-contamination with gluten should be assumed and Kacto should not be treated as celiac-safe without a direct conversation with the staff.

The food is described as modern American 'with a Japanese twist,' so Japanese-style seasonings are used in some dishes. Most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat, meaning sauces, marinades, and Japanese-accented dishes are likely sources of hidden gluten. No wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned in any source.

The kitchen centers on eggs, dairy (pancakes, smoothies, truffled eggs), beef burgers, and steak. There is no documented vegan menu or vegan prep separation, so cross-contact with egg, dairy, and meat should be expected and any plant-based request needs to be confirmed in advance with the staff.
Service is described as friendly and generally efficient, and most servers speak some English, which makes it easier to ask detailed questions about ingredients and allergens before ordering.

name: Au petit Foreau pâtissière (オ・プチフォロ・パティシエール)

claims.text: Entire shop is wheat-free: all products are gluten-free and rice-flour (米粉) based, with no wheat flour used on the premises (全商品グルテンフリー＆プラントベース). This structurally minimizes wheat cross-contact, but no explicit celiac-grade cross-contamination protocol is published.
Patisserie only — no savory soy-sauce dishes. The 0% cheesecake uses white miso (白味噌) and kuzu; miso can be a hidden wheat/barley source, so confirm the miso is GF if highly sensitive.
No animal products are used anywhere in the shop (fully plant-based), so animal cross-contact is not a concern.

Owner-run allergy-focused patisserie; individual products are also flagged for specific allergies (e.g. ヴィーガン・小麦フリー, 乳・小麦フリー) on the owner's blog, indicating allergy awareness. Orders are handled directly by the chef via pre-order.
Dedicated gluten-free + plant-based facility using rice flour, organic ingredients and no white sugar; signature 0% cheesecake is gluten/white-sugar/animal 0%.
Trusted enough by the vegan/GF community that mumokuteki cafe and Cafe Ren resell her sweets.
